title: YOU CAN HEAR SERMONS EVERY SUNDAY AND STILL BE LYING TO YOUR OWN SOUL
paragraphs: YOU CAN HEAR SERMONS EVERY SUNDAY AND STILL BE LYING TO YOUR OWN SOUL
James exposed a terrifying kind of spiritual deception: the person who knows God's Word, loves hearing it, and still refuses to let it change the way they live.
There is something more frightening than a sinner who knows he is lost.
It is a religious person who is absolutely convinced he is spiritually healthy because he never misses a sermon.
He knows when to say amen.
He knows which worship songs bring tears to his eyes.
He can recognize false teaching, quote his favorite Bible verses, and explain what other Christians need to change.
But there is one person he has become dangerously skilled at avoiding.
Himself.
And perhaps the most unsettling thing about this story is that the person James is warning us about might not be sitting across the church from you.
He might be sitting in your seat.
Holding your Bible.
Reading these very words.
Before you become offended, please understand something.
This is not an attack on people who attend church faithfully. Gathering with believers, listening to Scripture, and receiving biblical teaching are beautiful and necessary parts of Christian life.
But what if something meant to bring us closer to God has quietly become something we use to convince ourselves that we are already close enough?
What if we have mistaken exposure to truth for surrender to truth?
And what if the greatest danger is not that we have stopped listening to God, but that we have learned how to listen without obeying?
James did not leave that question unanswered.
He wrote:
“But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves.” — James 1:22, KJV
Read that again.
Not because it is complicated.
Because it is painfully clear.
James does not say that people who merely hear God's Word are necessarily deceiving everyone around them.
He says they are deceiving themselves.
And that is a different kind of tragedy.
Because when someone else lies to you, there is at least a possibility that you will discover the deception.
But when you become the person manufacturing your own spiritual excuses, you can spend years defending a condition that desperately needs healing.
You can become an expert at recognizing everybody else's sin while remaining remarkably comfortable with your own.
You can applaud a sermon on forgiveness and still refuse to release the bitterness you have been feeding for years.
You can cry when the pastor speaks about holiness, then return home and willingly entertain the same secret compromise.
You can raise your hands during worship while using those same hands to type words that humiliate, destroy, or wound another human being.
You can talk beautifully about grace while showing almost none to the people who live under your roof.
And you can do all of this while genuinely believing that your spiritual life is growing.
That is why James's warning is so serious.
It confronts the terrifying possibility that we can become emotionally familiar with truth without becoming obedient to it.
The original Greek makes this even more revealing.
James writes:
Γίνεσθε δὲ ποιηταὶ λόγου καὶ μὴ μόνον ἀκροαταί, παραλογιζόμενοι ἑαυτούς.
Ginesthe de poiētai logou kai mē monon akroatai, paralogizomenoi heautous.
The meaning is:
“But become doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving yourselves.”
Notice the word γίνεσθε (ginesthe).
It carries the sense of becoming or being. James is calling believers into a continuing way of life characterized by obedience.
Not a single emotional response.
Not one impressive Sunday.
Not one dramatic moment at the altar.
A life increasingly shaped by the Word of God.
Then there is the Greek word παραλογιζόμενοι (paralogizomenoi), translated “deceiving.”
It conveys the idea of misleading oneself through faulty reasoning.
Think about that.
A person can construct a convincing spiritual argument that excuses the very disobedience Scripture is confronting.
“I attend church. Surely I am doing fine.”
“I know the Bible. Surely I am mature.”
“I serve in ministry. Surely God is pleased with everything else in my life.”
“I am not as bad as that person.”
“I will deal with this sin when life becomes easier.”
But the ability to explain away disobedience does not make disobedience disappear.
And spiritual activity cannot substitute for surrender.
There is a kind of deception that does not begin with rejecting Scripture.
It begins with hearing Scripture and quietly deciding that its demands are meant for somebody else.
James continues with an image so ordinary that almost anyone can understand it.

“For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was.” — James 1:23–24, KJV
Imagine waking up one morning.
You walk toward the mirror.
Your hair is a mess. Your face is dirty. There is something on your cheek that you somehow failed to notice.
The mirror shows you exactly what needs attention.
You stare at it.
You agree with it.
You might even compliment the mirror for being so accurate.
Then you walk away.
And change absolutely nothing.
The problem was never the mirror.
The problem was your response to what the mirror revealed.
That is what Scripture does.
It reveals things we might otherwise prefer not to see.
Our pride.
Our selfishness.
Our bitterness.
Our hidden motives.
Our carefully protected idols.
Our desperate need for the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And sometimes the most dangerous response to that revelation is not anger.
It is admiration without action.
“What a powerful sermon.”
“What an incredible message.”
“That preacher really spoke the truth today.”
Then Monday arrives.
And the mirror is forgotten.
The apology is never made.
The dishonesty continues.
The neglected family member remains neglected.
The private sin is carefully hidden again.
The person who needed compassion receives another excuse.
And another week passes.
Then another Sunday comes.
Another sermon.
Another emotional moment.
Another promise to change.
Until conviction itself becomes familiar enough that we no longer feel compelled to respond.
That should disturb us.
Not because every struggle means we are hypocrites.
But because there is an enormous difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
A believer may fall and grieve deeply over that fall.
A believer may battle the same temptation repeatedly while sincerely seeking God's help.
A believer may be weak, exhausted, confused, and still genuinely walking toward Christ.
James is not demanding sinless perfection.
He is confronting the dangerous separation of hearing God's truth from responding to it.
And that distinction matters.
Because the Gospel is not the announcement that Jesus saves people who have already perfected their obedience.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners who could never rescue themselves.
But the grace that forgives us is not permission to remain indifferent to the God who saved us.
Jesus Himself asked a question that should stop every religious person in their tracks.
“And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?” — Luke 6:46, KJV
There it is.
The painful contradiction.
We can say “Lord” with our mouths while resisting His lordship in our choices.
We can praise His authority in a worship service while treating His commands as optional in our private lives.
We can sing about surrender while protecting the one thing we refuse to surrender.
And somehow convince ourselves that the song was enough.
But Jesus did not come merely to collect religious compliments.
He came to reconcile sinners to God.
He came to forgive, redeem, restore, and transform.
He came to call people out of darkness and into His marvelous light.
And sometimes that journey begins with the uncomfortable discovery that we have been using religious familiarity to hide from genuine repentance.
Maybe this is where the article becomes personal.
Because perhaps you remember a sermon that made you uncomfortable.
Not because the preacher was harsh.
But because the Word of God seemed to find the one locked room inside your heart.
You knew exactly what needed to change.
You knew whom you needed to forgive.
You knew which relationship needed boundaries.
You knew which habit was poisoning your spiritual life.
You knew which lie needed to be confessed.
For a moment, you felt exposed.
You promised God that things would be different.
And then you walked outside.
Your phone buzzed.
Life resumed.
The conviction faded.
And the decision you knew you needed to make was postponed again.
Perhaps nobody noticed.
Perhaps you even forgot about it.
But God did not stop loving you when you walked away from that moment.
And His Word did not become less true because you delayed your response.
That is why this warning is not simply frightening.
It is merciful.
God is allowing us to see what we might otherwise spend a lifetime refusing to confront.
And there is grace in being exposed before our excuses become our prison.
James does not end his illustration with a person who forgets the mirror.
He describes another response.
“But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.” — James 1:25, KJV
The Greek expression νόμον τέλειον τὸν τῆς ἐλευθερίας (nomon teleion ton tēs eleutherias) means “the perfect law, the law of liberty.”
James is not teaching that we purchase salvation by accumulating good deeds.
He is describing the blessed life of someone who receives God's truth and continues in it rather than treating it as a passing religious experience.
God's Word does not become a prison when we obey it.
It exposes the things that have been imprisoning us.
The bitterness we thought was protecting us.
The pride we mistook for strength.
The secret sin we called harmless.
The greed we disguised as ambition.
The cruelty we justified because someone had hurt us first.
Sin often promises freedom while quietly tightening its chains.
But Jesus said:
“If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed.” — John 8:36, KJV
That freedom is not the ability to do whatever our sinful desires demand.
It is freedom from sin's condemning guilt and enslaving dominion through the saving work of Christ.
And it changes the way we hear His Word.
We no longer approach Scripture merely asking, “Was that sermon good?”
We begin asking, “Lord, what are You showing me about my heart, and how must I respond?”
That question can change a marriage.
It can restore honesty to a friendship.
It can transform the atmosphere inside a home.
It can turn a religious routine into a genuine walk with Jesus.
And sometimes it begins with something painfully small.
A sincere apology.
A confession without excuses.
A decision to stop feeding a destructive habit.
A phone call you have been avoiding.
An act of generosity when nobody is watching.
A quiet prayer in which you finally stop pretending.
Not because these actions earn the love of God.
But because His grace is teaching you to live differently.
And here is where we must be especially careful.
There is a terrible way to misunderstand James.
We can read his warning, become frightened, and begin believing that God will accept us only when our obedience becomes impressive enough.
But that is not the Gospel.
The apostle Paul writes:
Salvation is God's gift.
Not our achievement.
Not our church attendance.
Not our ability to quote Scripture.
Not our moral résumé.
Not our financial generosity.
Not even our most impressive acts of religious service.
We are saved through faith in Jesus Christ by grace.
And Paul immediately continues:
“For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.” — Ephesians 2:10, KJV
Do you see the beautiful order?
We are not saved by good works.
We are saved for good works.
Obedience is not the price of redemption.
It is the fruit of a life being transformed by the Redeemer.
That is why James and Paul are not enemies.
Paul confronts the idea that human works can earn salvation.
James confronts the idea that a claimed faith can remain permanently barren of obedience.
Both point us away from spiritual self-confidence and toward the living reality of faith in Christ.
And perhaps nobody illustrates that reality more beautifully than a man who once denied knowing Jesus.
Peter.
He had heard the teachings.
He had witnessed the miracles.
He had walked beside the Savior.
He had confidently declared that he would remain faithful even if others fell away.
Yet when the pressure came, Peter denied Jesus three times.
Imagine the horror of realizing that your courage was not nearly as strong as your confession.
Imagine hearing the rooster.
Remembering the words of Jesus.
And realizing what you had done.
Luke tells us that Peter went out and wept bitterly.
This was not a man who needed another impressive religious performance.
He needed mercy.
He needed restoration.
He needed the Savior he had failed.
And after the resurrection, in John 21, Jesus met Peter again.
Not to pretend the denial had never happened.
Not to declare betrayal harmless.
But to restore a fallen disciple and entrust him with responsibility.
Jesus repeatedly asked Peter whether he loved Him.
And He called Peter to care for His sheep.
Love for Christ was not meant to remain a beautiful declaration.
It was to become a life of faithful response.
That is the heart of this message.
Jesus does not expose our failures merely to leave us ashamed. He calls us to Himself so that grace can produce what religious appearances never could.
Perhaps you have failed in ways nobody knows.
Perhaps you have spent years looking spiritually strong while privately falling apart.
Perhaps your family has seen a version of you that the people in church would hardly recognize.
Perhaps you have preached patience while losing your temper at home.
Perhaps you have spoken about purity while fighting a secret battle.
Perhaps you have encouraged others to trust God while quietly drowning in fear.
And now you are wondering whether you have been deceiving yourself all along.
Do not run from that question.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because the answer to spiritual deception is not another layer of religious pretending.
It is truth.
Repentance.
Faith.
And the mercy of the Savior who already knows everything you have been trying to hide.

The Greek word commonly translated “repent” in the New Testament, μετανοέω (metanoeō), speaks of changing one's mind or turning in one's thinking. In the biblical call to repentance, this involves a genuine turning toward God that bears fruit in life.
Repentance is not simply feeling bad because a sermon made you emotional.
It is responding to God with a changed heart and direction.
And when we fall, we do not need to manufacture a flawless spiritual image.
We need to return to Christ.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” — 1 John 1:9, KJV
There is no need to hide from the One who gave His life to redeem sinners.
At the cross, Jesus bore sin's judgment.
Through His resurrection, He conquered death.
And through faith in Him, guilty people can receive forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
This is why the Gospel is greater than religious self-improvement.
Jesus did not come merely to make bad people behave a little better.
He came to save the lost.
To make the spiritually dead alive.
To bring sinners into a restored relationship with the Father.
To create a people who, by the Holy Spirit, increasingly reflect His character.
And if you are reading this with tears in your eyes because you recognize yourself in James's warning, hear this carefully.
Your failure does not have to be the final chapter.
Your hidden sin does not have to remain your secret master.
Your spiritual complacency does not have to become your permanent identity.
There is still mercy in Christ.
There is still a call to repentance.
There is still a Savior who receives those who come to Him in faith.
But do not confuse that invitation with permission to delay forever.
The same Jesus who welcomes sinners calls them to follow Him.
Not merely to admire Him.
Not merely to study Him.
Not merely to discuss Him.
To follow Him.
So when the next sermon ends, resist the temptation to measure its success only by how deeply it moved you.
Ask what truth you need to obey.
When Scripture confronts your pride, humble yourself.
When it exposes dishonesty, tell the truth.
When it calls you to forgive, begin taking the steps of forgiveness, even when healing and rebuilding trust require time.
When it calls you to love, remember the person who has been receiving your impatience instead.
When it exposes a destructive habit, seek the help and accountability you need rather than promising yourself that tomorrow will somehow be different.
When it reveals your sin, confess it to God and turn toward Christ.
And when you discover that you are weaker than you imagined, remember that your hope was never supposed to rest in your own strength.
It rests in Jesus.
The One who forgives.
The One who restores.
The One who gives His Spirit to help His people walk in newness of life.
You do not need to become the hero of your own redemption story.
You need the Redeemer.
And that brings us to a question I hope stays with you long after you close this article.
What is the one thing God has already shown you through His Word that you keep postponing?
Not what your pastor needs to change.
Not what your spouse needs to understand.
Not what the people in your church need to hear.
You.
What truth have you been admiring instead of obeying?
What apology remains trapped behind your pride?
What compromise have you been protecting?
What command have you been treating as a suggestion?
What would your life look like if the next truth you heard from Scripture became more than another inspiring moment?
You may not be able to repair everything tonight.
You may need wise counsel, time, support, and the help of other believers.
But you can begin with an honest response to God.

“Lord Jesus, I have heard Your Word so many times. Forgive me for the times I used religious knowledge to excuse a disobedient heart. Expose what I have been hiding. Give me the humility to repent, the faith to trust Your grace, and the strength through Your Spirit to obey. I do not want to be merely impressed by Your truth. I want my life to be changed by You. Amen.”
And if this message has reached a place in your heart you have been avoiding, do not let the moment disappear into another forgotten scroll.
You do not have to reveal private details to strangers. But perhaps a simple, honest comment can become the beginning of encouragement and prayer.
And if God has already been changing your life, share a testimony. Someone else may need to know that repentance is not the end of hope. It can be the beginning of restoration.
There may be someone on your Facebook friends list who attends church every Sunday but is quietly drifting away from the Lord.
Someone who knows the language of Christianity but has forgotten the joy of walking closely with Jesus.
Someone who is ashamed of a hidden battle and believes there is no way back.
Because faith is not meant to be nourished by one emotional moment and then abandoned until the following Sunday.
We need God's Word continually.
We need sound teaching.
We need Christian fellowship.
We need to be reminded of the cross, the resurrection, and the grace that calls us into a transformed life.
That is part of why Gospel Warrior exists.
And if this ministry has helped you grow closer to Jesus, I want to invite you to consider something more than simply reading another article.
Not because financial support can purchase God's favor.
And certainly not because you must pay a ministry in order to glorify God.
But freely and prayerfully supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful expression of Christian generosity.
Paul reminds believers:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV
It can help sustain the writing, teaching, encouragement, and outreach that make messages like this possible.
Inviting others to follow can introduce them to Scripture and resources they might never have encountered otherwise.
These items are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
They are simply additional ways to encourage faith, share biblical messages, and express our appreciation to those helping this work continue.
That library reflects something we deeply believe.
The Word of God should never be treated as a luxury reserved for those who can afford to pay.
The Gospel is not for sale.
And God's grace is not locked behind a payment screen.
If Gospel Warrior has strengthened your faith, helped you understand Scripture, or encouraged you during a difficult season, please consider joining those who support its continued growth.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Grow.
Keep walking with Jesus.
Because the purpose of every article, every resource, every book, and every invitation is ultimately the same.
Not to build admiration for a ministry.
But to point people toward the Savior.
And now, before you leave, I want to return to the warning that started this entire conversation.
James was not writing about people who had never heard the truth.
He was warning people who had heard it.
People who could recognize it.
People who might even agree with it.
But who were in danger of leaving it behind without obedience.
So perhaps the greatest question after reading this is not whether you enjoyed the article.
It is not whether it made you cry.
The question is whether you will respond to the Word of God.
Because a thousand sermons cannot substitute for one surrendered heart.
A thousand emotional moments cannot replace repentance.
And a lifetime of religious familiarity cannot save anyone apart from Jesus Christ.
The thief on the cross did not have years to build a record of religious achievement. He turned to Jesus in faith, and Jesus promised him paradise (Luke 23:39–43).
That is grace.
But the person who has heard the truth for decades must never mistake the number of sermons attended for the reality of saving faith.
That is James's warning.
And the invitation of the Gospel remains open.
Come to Christ.
Trust Him.
Confess your sins.
Receive His mercy.
And by the power of His Spirit, begin walking in the truth you have heard.
Perhaps your story has been filled with failure, secrecy, pride, broken promises, or years of spiritual pretending.
That does not have to be how it ends.
The same Jesus who restored Peter still calls sinners to repentance and faith.
The same Gospel that exposes our need reveals the Savior who is sufficient for it.
And the same Word that confronts our self-deception points us toward the truth that sets us free.
The saddest thing would not be discovering today that you have been deceiving yourself. It would be hearing God's warning, recognizing His mercy, and walking away unchanged once again.
